summary: This manuscript explores a variational quantum formulation for nonlinear elasticity problems arising from hyperelastic material models, targeting near term noisy intermediate scale quantum (NISQ) devices. The approach leverages the potential energy structure of hyperelasticity and employs a hybrid quantum classical framework in which the energy functional is evaluated using parameterized quantum circuits and optimized through classical routines. To enable implementation on current quantum hardware, polynomial approximations of the nonlinear strain energy density are introduced, yielding a representation compatible with variational quantum algorithms. The methodology is demonstrated on a one dimensional NeoHookean material model using finite element discretizations with first and second order shape functions and nonhomogeneous boundary conditions. Numerical experiments investigate the influence of the polynomial approximation order on the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed approach, illustrating its feasibility for near term quantum devices.

AI.tldr: The manuscript presents a variational quantum method for tackling nonlinear elasticity in hyperelastic materials using near term quantum devices.
AI.motivation: To harness quantum computing for solving complex nonlinear elasticity problems that are challenging for classical methods.
AI.method: Combines variational quantum algorithms with classical optimization, utilizing polynomial approximations for strain energy density in hyperelastic models, implemented on NISQ devices.
AI.result: The method was practically demonstrated on a NeoHookean material model, with varying polynomial orders affecting accuracy and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach is feasible for current quantum hardware, suggesting a pathway for practical applications in material science.

title: Fundamental limitations on entanglement extraction from purity
summary: States of sufficiently low purity are separable and cannot be entangled by unital (purity-non-generating) operations. Since high-purity states are experimentally demanding, it is natural to ask how much purity a state must possess to enable entanglement generation. Absolutely separable states remain separable under all deterministic unital channels, and so cannot deterministically generate entanglement in this setting. We show, however, that some absolutely separable states can generate entanglement via probabilistic protocols that do not produce purity. This motivates the study of states that fail to generate entanglement with any non-zero probability, which we call completely absolutely separable; we give a full characterization of this class. Along the way, we derive a novel sufficient condition for separability that depends only on the largest and smallest eigenvalues, along with the smallest local dimension and is independent of all previously known spectral separability criteria.

AI.tldr: The study investigates the purity threshold required for generating entanglement, identifying types of separable states and introducing a new criterion for separability based only on eigenvalues.
AI.motivation: To determine the minimum purity required for a state to facilitate entanglement generation, given the experimental challenges of high-purity states.
AI.method: The authors characterize a new class of states termed 'completely absolutely separable' and derive a sufficient condition for separability based on eigenvalues and local dimensions.
AI.result: Some absolutely separable states can generate entanglement through probabilistic protocols; a new sufficient condition for separability is established.
AI.conclusion: The research enhances the understanding of separability and entanglement generation, providing new tools for analyzing quantum states.

title: Hybrid Gaussian-exponential zero-noise extrapolation for periodic circuits
summary: Zero-noise extrapolation provides a practical means of suppressing gate errors in current noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware. The accuracy of the zero-noise estimate depends sensitively on the fidelity of the assumed noise model to the actual error scaling. This work introduces a hybrid Gaussian-exponential extrapolation scheme tailored for quantum circuits with periodic structure, which are ubiquitous in quantum algorithms. Under Pauli diagonal errors, by constructing and analyzing an approximate Markov process for the transfer of Pauli operators, we prove a central limit theorem: the noise amplification factor weakly approaches a log-normal distribution, which motivates augmenting the standard exponential model with Gaussian variance corrections. The resulting model requires no prior noise characterization and applies directly to arbitrary periodic circuits. Performance is assessed on Trotterized Ising dynamics, random circuits, and Grover search algorithm using Qiskit noise simulators. For moderate to large circuit depths, the hybrid model yields measurable reductions in bias relative to previous extrapolation variants, indicating its utility for error mitigation on near-term quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a hybrid extrapolation method reducing gate errors in quantum circuits by enhancing noise modeling without prior characterization.
AI.motivation: To improve the accuracy of zero-noise extrapolation methods amidst varying error models in quantum computing.
AI.method: A hybrid Gaussian-exponential extrapolation scheme is developed, specifically for circuits with periodic structures, incorporating a log-normal distribution for noise amplification.
AI.result: The new model shows significant bias reductions in error mitigation for various quantum algorithms, outperforming existing techniques.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid approach enhances performance in error suppression on current quantum hardware, demonstrating practical applicability.

title: Permutation Matrix Representation for Quantum Simulation: Comparative Resource Analysis
summary: We present a comparative study of the permutation matrix representation (PMR) method for Hamiltonian simulation alongside other leading quantum algorithms. Our analysis focuses on resource costs for simulating both time-independent and time-dependent Hamiltonians. For the time-independent case, we benchmark PMR against quantum signal processing (QSP) and qubitization, using the Rydberg interaction Hamiltonian as a representative example. For the time-dependent case, we compare the time-dependent extension of PMR with the quantum highly oscillatory protocol (qHOP), applied to a Floquet-driven transverse field Ising model in arbitrary spatial dimensions. In both regimes, we find that PMR offers complementary advantages in resource requirements and exhibits favorable scaling with certain system parameters, suggesting that it may provide practical benefits on resource-constrained quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper compares the permutation matrix representation method for Hamiltonian simulation with other quantum algorithms, highlighting its advantages in resource efficiency in both time-independent and time-dependent regimes.
AI.motivation: The study aims to evaluate the efficiency of the PMR method against established quantum algorithms, particularly focusing on resource costs in quantum simulations.
AI.method: The comparison involves benchmarking PMR against quantum signal processing (QSP) and qubitization for time-independent Hamiltonians, and against the quantum highly oscillatory protocol (qHOP) for time-dependent Hamiltonians.
AI.result: PMR shows complementary advantages, offering better resource efficiency and scaling with certain system parameters compared to other methods.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest that PMR could be beneficial for practical applications on resource-constrained quantum hardware.

title: Candidate collapse-noise correlators from Generalized Trace Dynamics: a Hubble-scale spectral line under structural assumptions
summary:
We present a conditional construction of candidate CSL-type collapse-noise correlators inspired by Generalized Trace Dynamics (GTD). The construction is not a parameter-free derivation from the minimal GTD Grassmann algebra. It rests on a chain of explicit structural postulates, listed in Section 1; within that auxiliary structure the spectral form and amplitude follow by computation rather than by phenomenological fitting. The resulting narrow-band spectrum at the Hubble scale lies outside the bands of current CSL bounds, so the framework is not in tension with existing high-frequency data.
  We compute the two-point function of a candidate collapse-noise operator associated with the GTD aikyon decomposition $q_i = q_B + a_0β_i q_F$. In the minimal Grassmann algebra, $q_F$ appears only multiplied by Grassmann generators $β_i$, the reduction of $\mathrm{Tr}(q_F^\daggerΓ^μq_F)$ to ghost-mode operators is obstructed by the nilpotent $δβ= β_2 - β_1$, and the pure-fermion coefficient $β_1β_2$ has no ordinary sign, modulus, or inverse. We therefore introduce an auxiliary canonical fermionic Fock-space sector for $q_F$, equivalently replacing the nilpotent pure-fermion coefficient by an ordinary effective scalar body parameter. This replacement is an independent structural postulate, not a consequence of the original minimal action.
  Under this auxiliary postulate, together with a scalar bilinear $J = \mathrm{Tr}(q_F^\dagger q_F)$ as bath operator, positive-norm canonical quantization, and an effective sign choice $σ= \pm1$ for the scalarized pure-fermion sector, elementary Wick contraction gives a Wightman line at $|ω| = 2ω_0$ with amplitude $A_J = (\hbar/2m_Rω_0 L_{\mathrm{aik}}^2)^2\cdot N\cdot D$. The cosmological identification $ω_0 \sim H_0$ places the line at twice the Hubble scale. [truncated]

AI.tldr: The paper presents a structure for collapse-noise correlators using Generalized Trace Dynamics (GTD), establishing a method that deviates from minimal GTD through structural postulates, yielding a spectrum at the Hubble scale that's not constrained by existing CSL bounds.
AI.motivation: To develop a framework for candidate CSL-type collapse-noise correlators that is rooted in a robust mathematical structure rather than phenomenological fitting.
AI.method: The method involves constructing a two-point function for a collapse-noise operator using a modified Grassmann algebra and specific structural postulates, leading to effective quantum treatments with canonical quantization.
AI.result: The resulting calculations indicate a narrow-band spectrum at the Hubble scale, consistent with cosmological parameters and avoiding conflict with current CSL bounds.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a new perspective on collapse-noise correlators with implications for cosmological scales, illustrating a shift from traditional minimal forms based on the introduction of auxiliary structures.

title: Total, quantum, and classical measures of anticoherence for mixed spin states
summary: Anticoherent spin states have isotropic low-order spin moments and are relevant to direction-independent metrology and quantum reference-frame alignment. In contrast to pure states, for mixed states such isotropy may originate either from genuine quantum correlations or from classical statistical mixing. We introduce an axiomatic framework for mixed-state $t$-anticoherence based on the symmetric qubit embedding. We distinguish total $t$-anticoherence, non-decreasing under SU(2)-covariant channels, from quantum $t$-anticoherence, defined as a resource monotone relative to a chosen total measure and constrained to coincide with it on pure states. This yields a classical contribution as their difference. We construct total measures based on reduced-state purity, Hilbert-Schmidt distance, and cumulative multipoles, and we discuss fidelity-based total candidates. We construct quantum counterparts via convex-roof extensions of pure-state functionals tied to bipartite entanglement in the symmetric sector. We provide explicit mixed-state examples, identify states with maximal quantum anticoherence supported on anticoherent subspaces, study robustness under particle loss for different types of states, and characterize the trade-off between purity and the maximal achievable anticoherence order.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framework for analyzing mixed-state anticoherent spin states, distinguishing between classical and quantum contributions to their isotropy.
AI.motivation: The study aims to explore the nature of anticoherent spin states and their applications in quantum metrology and reference-frame alignment, especially in relation to mixed states.
AI.method: An axiomatic framework for mixed-state $t$-anticoherence is proposed, distinguishing total and quantum $t$-anticoherence using symmetric qubit embedding and measures based on state purity and entanglement.
AI.result: The paper elucidates explicit mixed-state examples, identifies states with maximal quantum anticoherence, and examines robustness against particle loss, along with a trade-off analysis between purity and anticoherence order.
AI.conclusion: The findings enhance the understanding of anticoherent states, contributing to the development of quantum technologies by clarifying the distinction between quantum and classical contributions to isotropy.

title: High-Fidelity ROI CT Reconstruction with Limited Quantum Resources via Hybrid Classical-Quantum Refinement
summary: Quantum optimization for computed tomography (CT) reconstruction is constrained by the number of binary variables required for image representation, making direct whole-image quantum reconstruction difficult for large or structurally complex objects. We propose a hybrid region-of-interest (ROI) refinement framework in which a coarse global image is first reconstructed by quantum tomographic reconstruction (QTR) and quantum compressed sensing tomographic reconstruction (QCSTR), filtered backprojection (FBP), or simultaneous algebraic reconstruction technique (SART), and quantum optimization is then applied only to the selected ROI through a residual projection-image formulation. This strategy reduces the effective QUBO size while preserving high-fidelity reconstruction in the target region. Experiments on three discrete phantom samples show that both QTR/QCSTR+QTR/QCSTR and SART+QTR/QCSTR achieve accurate ROI reconstruction for moderate-size cases under a reduced-angle setting. For the largest and most complex sample, the quality of the coarse global estimate becomes critical, and the best result is obtained when a stable classical coarse reconstruction is combined with second-stage ROI-only QTR/QCSTR. Among the tested pipelines, SART+QTR/QCSTR achieves the lowest average ROI RMSE and MAE. The results indicate that the practical advantage of quantum-assisted CT reconstruction lies in reserving quantum optimization for local refinement while using classical reconstruction to stabilize the global background.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a hybrid quantum optimization framework for CT reconstruction that focuses on region-of-interest (ROI) refinement to enhance image quality while managing variable constraints effectively.
AI.motivation: Traditional quantum optimization methods struggle with large or complex objects in CT reconstruction due to the high number of binary variables needed for full image representation.
AI.method: A two-stage approach is proposed: first, a global image is reconstructed using classical or quantum methods, followed by quantum optimization focusing on a selected ROI to refine the image.
AI.result: Experiments indicate that the proposed method achieves accurate ROI reconstructions, with SART combined with quantum methods showing the lowest reconstruction errors for moderate-size cases.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that utilizing classical methods for global reconstruction while reserving quantum techniques for local ROI refinement optimizes CT imaging outcomes.

title: Near surface donor-acceptor pairs in hydrogenated homoepitaxial diamond nanolayers
comment: Main text: 17 pages, 5 figures Supplementary information: 1 page, 2 figures
summary: Hydrogen-terminated diamond is known for its p-type surface conductivity, which arises from a near-surface hole accumulation layer induced by adsorbed acceptor species. Here, we demonstrate that these surface acceptors also form optically active donor-acceptor pairs (DAP) with substitutional nitrogen donors in diamond. The insertion of a nominally undoped CVD interlayer between a nitrogen-rich HPHT substrate and a hydrogen-terminated surface enables the precise tuning of the donor-acceptor separation with nanometer precision. Radiative DAP recombination appears as bright, spectrally narrow lines whose intensity, energy, and decay dynamics depend systematically on interlayer thickness. Individual lines show single-photon statistics, while ensembles exhibit strong polarization anisotropy reflecting the planar donor-acceptor geometry. These findings reveal an optical counterpart of hydrogen-induced surface transfer doping in diamond and establish a surface-defined, nanometer-tunable platform for engineering DAP-based quantum emitters.

AI.tldr: Hydrogen-terminated diamond exhibits p-type surface conductivity through hole accumulation. This study shows that surface acceptors can form optically active DAPs with nitrogen donors, with interlayer thickness enabling tunable donor-acceptor separation and unique optical properties.
AI.motivation: The research aims to explore the optical properties of hydrogen-terminated diamond surfaces and their interaction with nitrogen donors to enhance quantum emitter technologies.
AI.method: A nominally undoped CVD interlayer was inserted between a nitrogen-rich HPHT substrate and a hydrogen-terminated surface, allowing precise control over the donor-acceptor separation.
AI.result: Bright, narrow DAP recombination lines were observed, with characteristics varying according to the interlayer thickness, demonstrating single-photon statistics and polarization anisotropy.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals a link between surface transfer doping and optical activity in diamond, establishing a platform for tunable DAP-based quantum emitters.

title: Quantum Markovian Dynamics from a Double Covariance Stochastic Framework
summary: We develop an interacting extension of the Double Covariance Model (DCM), a stochastic subquantum framework in which macroscopic quantum dynamics emerge through coarse-graining of correlated microscopic fluctuations. Starting from local stochastic differential equations on subsystem Hilbert spaces, we derive a closed evolution equation for a coarse-grained double covariance operator using multi-scale Itô calculus and sliding-window averaging. The construction explicitly incorporates two separated temporal scales: a fast microscopic fluctuation scale governing subquantum stochastic processes and a slower macroscopic observation scale associated with coarse-grained dynamics. Within the hydrodynamic limit, where the ratio between microscopic correlation time and averaging-window scale vanishes, rapidly fluctuating corrections disappear and the effective dynamics converges to a deterministic macroscopic transport equation. We show that the emergent macroscopic dynamics has the exact Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad (GKSL) form: coherent Hamiltonian evolution arises from deterministic subquantum flow, while dissipative channels emerge from quadratic noise correlations. The framework further demonstrates how non-separable interaction Hamiltonians can arise from strictly local, state-dependent stochastic feedback fields. In the fluctuation-free limit, the model reduces naturally to the standard von Neumann equation, providing a unified stochastic foundation for both open and closed quantum dynamics.

AI.tldr: Development of the Double Covariance Model (DCM) to describe macroscopic quantum dynamics through microscopic fluctuations and coarse-graining.
AI.motivation: To create a comprehensive framework that transitions from stochastic microscopic behaviors to deterministic macroscopic phenomena in quantum systems.
AI.method: Introduced a closed evolution equation via multi-scale Itô calculus and sliding-window averaging, accounting for fast and slow temporal scales in dynamics.
AI.result: The emergent dynamics follows the GKSL form, with Hamiltonian evolution from deterministic flow and dissipative channels from noise correlations; the model also shows how non-separable interactions can arise from local feedback.
AI.conclusion: The model integrates both open and closed quantum dynamics, reducing to the von Neumann equation in the fluctuation-free limit.

title: Performance Analysis of Underwater Quantum Key Distribution Protocols: BB84, SARG04, and BBM92
summary: Underwater quantum key distribution (UQKD) ensures unconditional communication security based on the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics. This study examines the performance of the BB84, SARG04, and the entanglement-based BBM92 protocols under the impact of both system optical parameters and the physical effects of the underwater channel. The main performance criteria considered are the quantum bit error rate (QBER) and the quantum correlation between the communicating parties as functions of the propagation distance in three types of non-turbulent seawater: clear, coastal, and turbid. For the BBM92 protocol, the quantum channel is modeled using Kraus operators, which characterize the combined effects of attenuation and depolarization on maximally-entangled photons, allowing the derivation of our analytical expression of the QBER, based on the correlation losses between measurements. Monte Carlo simulation results validate the analytical expression of the QBER for all the studied protocols, under various water types, atmospheric conditions, and system parameters. The results determine the conditions under which QKD protocols achieve optimal performance for secure and efficient underwater quantum communications.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates the performance of three underwater quantum key distribution protocols under different seawater conditions, focusing on quantum bit error rates and channel correlations.
AI.motivation: To ensure secure quantum communication in underwater environments where traditional methods may fail due to channel impairments.
AI.method: Analyzed BB84, SARG04, and BBM92 protocols using a model for quantum channel impacts with Kraus operators; validated results through Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.result: Analytical expressions for the quantum bit error rate were derived and validated, showing how performance varies with water type and conditions.
AI.conclusion: Identified optimal conditions for achieving effective and secure underwater quantum communications across different protocols.

title: Non-Clifford Crosstalk Noise in Surface Codes Using Hybrid Stabilizer-Tensor Network Methods
summary: Scalable realisation of quantum computing is reliant on the development of fault tolerant devices. Analysis of quantum error correction protocols typically considers incoherent noise models or noise-free syndrome measurements. While this is simple to simulate classically and straightforward to compute analytically, these simplifications are unable to capture the full dynamics of a noisy quantum system. In this work we use advanced hybrid stabilizer-tensor network simulation techniques to simulate coherent quantum crosstalk noise during syndrome extraction on a surface code. We show that the inclusion of coherence increases logical error rates and lowers the code threshold. In addition, we show that the specific distribution of the noise can quantitatively change logical error rates. The methods in this work allow simulation of quantum error correction with noise models previously inaccessible to classical simulation, providing new insights on the effect of crosstalk noise on quantum error correction codes.

AI.tldr: This paper explores the impact of coherent quantum crosstalk noise on quantum error correction, revealing increased logical error rates and lower code thresholds compared to traditional noise models.
AI.motivation: The work aims to address the limitations of classical simulations of quantum error correction by incorporating coherent noise models, which are often overlooked in existing analyses.
AI.method: The authors employ advanced hybrid stabilizer-tensor network simulation techniques to model the effects of coherent quantum crosstalk noise during syndrome extraction in a surface code framework.
AI.result: The inclusion of coherence in the noise models leads to higher logical error rates and a reduced code threshold, with the specific noise distribution significantly affecting the outcomes.
AI.conclusion: This research introduces a novel approach to simulate complex noise models, offering valuable insights into the challenges of quantum error correction in realistic noisy environments.

title: Ground-state estimation of the Heisenberg model on frustrated lattices with Sample-based Krylov Quantum Diagonalization
comment: 15 pages (11 pages main text + 4 pages appendix), 11 figures, 1 table
summary: Quantum spin simulations of frustrated lattices remain challenging for both classical and quantum algorithms, particularly in parameter regimes relevant to quantum spin liquid (QSL) phases. In this work, we apply Sample-based Krylov Quantum Diagonalization (SKQD) to estimate the ground state of the antiferromagnetic XXZ Heisenberg model on the $J_1$--$J_2$ square lattice, the Kagome lattice, and a 1D chain, studying system sizes from 12 to 72 spins. In our application of SKQD, we identify a ZZ deformation of $Δ=2$ as a sufficiently sparse Hamiltonian and introduce two modifications to the SKQD framework tailored to spin models: a canonical bitstring compression scheme that preserves the effectiveness of configuration recovery under spin-flip degeneracy, and the use of multiple Krylov subspaces to improve ground state coverage without any increase in quantum resources. For the 1D chain and Kagome lattice, SKQD achieves sub-percent ground-state energy errors at system sizes up to 24 spins, including a relative error of $0.002\%$ on the 12-site Kagome lattice, surpassing the best prior VQE result of $0.01\%$ on the same system while requiring no variational optimization. SKQD further extends to system sizes well beyond the reach of prior quantum algorithm studies, reaching 72 spins across all three geometries. Beyond 24 spins, accuracy degrades to relative errors of $19\%$--$36\%$ at 72 sites, but the gradual scaling of error with system size suggests these limits are set by available shot budgets and circuit depth rather than fundamental algorithmic constraints. Although classical tensor network methods remain state-of-the-art for these models, this work establishes a new benchmark for quantum simulation of the frustrated Heisenberg model and demonstrates SKQD as a scalable, hardware-compatible approach for studying strongly correlated spin systems.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SKQD to estimate the ground state of antiferromagnetic spin models, showing improved accuracy over prior VQE results and establishing a new benchmark for quantum simulations of frustrated lattices.
AI.motivation: To address challenges in simulating frustrated lattices relevant to quantum spin liquid phases using both classical and quantum algorithms.
AI.method: Sample-based Krylov Quantum Diagonalization (SKQD) applied to the antiferromagnetic XXZ Heisenberg model on various lattice geometries, with tailored modifications for spin models.
AI.result: SKQD achieves sub-percent energy errors for up to 24 spins, outperforming previous variational results. It extends the simulation capacity to 72 spins, though accuracy degrades beyond 24 spins.
AI.conclusion: SKQD provides a scalable, hardware-compatible method for quantum simulations of strongly correlated spin systems, setting a new benchmark despite accuracy limitations at larger sizes.

title: Rademacher Complexity Bounds for Parameterized Quantum Circuits Generated by Pauli Strings
summary: In this study, we analyze the Rademacher complexity $ \mathcal{R}_{M} $ of a parameterized unitary whose generators are chosen from $ n $-qubit Pauli strings. Although generalization bounds for quantum machine learning models have been studied in several settings, explicit Rademacher-complexity bounds for parameterized unitaries generated by Pauli strings remain less transparent. We derive simple scaling bounds in terms of the number of parameters $ L $ and the number of training samples $ M $: $ \mathcal{O}(\frac{L^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\sqrt{M}}) $ for the full parameter domain and $ \mathcal{O}(\frac{L}{\sqrt{M}}) $ for a restricted parameter domain. Furthermore, we compare the obtained results with those for a classical linear model class and suggest a potential statistical-complexity advantage when the norms of both the input and the parameter in the classical model scale with the number of parameters. Numerical experiments provide qualitative evidence consistent with the predicted scaling.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the Rademacher complexity of parameterized unitaries generated by Pauli strings, deriving scaling bounds and suggesting advantages over classical models.
AI.motivation: To clarify the understanding of Rademacher complexity in quantum machine learning, specifically for parameterized unitaries using Pauli strings, where existing bounds are less transparent.
AI.method: The study derives Rademacher complexity scaling bounds based on the number of parameters and training samples, providing explicit formulas for both full and restricted parameter domains.
AI.result: The derived complexity bounds are $	ext{O}( rac{L^{ rac{3}{2}}}{	ext{√}M})$ for the full parameter domain and $	ext{O}( rac{L}{	ext{√}M})$ for the restricted domain, demonstrating potential advantages over classical models.
AI.conclusion: Numerical experiments support the derived scaling results, indicating a possible statistical-complexity advantage in quantum models with norms scaling with parameters.

title: Quantum Subliminal Learning
summary: Machine learning models can inherit hidden behavioral traits through innocuous public interfaces, a phenomenon known as subliminal learning. Here we extend this framework to quantum models and study two distillation pathways: an auxiliary channel on random inputs and a restricted task channel in which the student matches a public supervised output while the hidden behavior resides on a disjoint task. Both classical and quantum neural networks (QNNs) exhibit efficient auxiliary-channel subliminal learning, but the task channel shows strong architecture dependence. Classical neural networks transmit little hidden-task information through the public-task interface, whereas QNNs retain most of the hidden-task signal. We show that a unified geometric picture explains both regimes: transmission is controlled by the teacher drift magnitude together with the fraction of hidden-task-relevant drift that remains visible through the public interface. These results identify a concrete security concern for quantum model supply chains and suggest a controlled route for hidden-information transfer in quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: This paper explores subliminal learning in quantum models, demonstrating distinct transmission characteristics in classical and quantum neural networks when learning from observable interfaces.
AI.motivation: To investigate the phenomenon of subliminal learning in machine learning models, particularly how it extends to quantum neural networks (QNNs).
AI.method: Analyzed two distillation pathways: an auxiliary channel on random inputs and a restricted task channel, examining the transmission of hidden behavioral traits for QNNs and classical neural networks.
AI.result: Classical neural networks transmit minimal hidden-task information through public-task interfaces, while QNNs retain most hidden-task signals, revealing architecture dependence in subliminal learning efficiency.
AI.conclusion: These findings raise security concerns for quantum model supply chains and offer insights into controlled hidden-information transfer in quantum information processing.

title: Bell's theorem: why probability factorisation fails
summary: The empirical proof of Bell inequality violations was a landmark moment for research into quantum foundations. It commits us to a universe without strict relativistic locality or requires that we escape through a potential loophole like many-worlds or superdeterminism. In this work, we consider a sequential, single-spin experiment whose auto-correlations match the two-spin entangled correlations of a Bell scenario. We use a counterfactual equivalence between the two to argue that Bell-type correlations are actually just a different implementation of the sequential experiment. This comports well with the counterfactual basis of the original EPR argument, and explains any apparent non-locality as a consequence of indirectly measuring quantities that do not have predefined values, due to the state-altering nature of sequential spin measurements.

AI.tldr: This paper explores a single-spin experiment providing insights into Bell inequality violations, suggesting that Bell-type correlations arise from sequential measurements rather than implying non-locality.
AI.motivation: To address the conceptual implications of Bell inequality violations and their connection to non-locality in quantum mechanics.
AI.method: The authors introduce a sequential, single-spin experiment and draw a counterfactual equivalence between its correlations and those observed in two-spin entangled systems.
AI.result: The findings indicate that Bell-type correlations can be viewed as a different manifestation of sequential measurements, thereby reframing our understanding of non-locality in quantum mechanics.
AI.conclusion: The apparent non-locality is explained as a result of measuring values that are not predefined, emphasizing the impact of the sequential nature of spin measurements.

title: Engineering recoil heating in coherent-scattering levitated optomechanics
summary: Recoil heating from photon scattering is a fundamental source of decoherence in optical trapping, severely limiting the preparation of nonclassical motional states. In cavity setups in the coherent scattering configuration, a predictive theory of recoil heating rate is missing, as usual perturbative approaches fail in the presence of sharp optical resonances. Hence, current works assume that the recoil heating rate is approximately equal to its free-space value. Here we show that this is not the case, as the electromagnetic environment can strongly modify recoil heating rate by the Purcell effect. Specifically, we predict that this rate can be significantly suppressed in state-of-the-art microcavities, for both center-of-mass and librational motion. To establish these results, we develop a general theoretical framework based on macroscopic quantum electrodynamics and on the few-mode quantization approach developed in nanophotonics. Our method applies to particles trapped in the presence of arbitrary electromagnetic structures, thus providing a route to engineering motional decoherence in levitated optomechanics by photonic structure design.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals that recoil heating from photon scattering in optical trapping can be significantly suppressed using microcavities, challenging existing assumptions about heating rates.
AI.motivation: Understanding and mitigating decoherence in optical trapping due to recoil heating is essential for preparing nonclassical motional states.
AI.method: A theoretical framework based on macroscopic quantum electrodynamics and few-mode quantization is developed to analyze the recoil heating rate in the presence of electromagnetic structures.
AI.result: The proposed method indicates that recoil heating rates can be substantially reduced in state-of-the-art microcavities, improving the prospects for nonclassical state preparation.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest that careful design of photonic structures can enhance control over motional decoherence in levitated optomechanics.

title: Error-corrected phase estimation averaged over variable grids on a trapped-ion quantum computer: hyperacuity spectra of a CO molecule adsorbed onto $χ$-Fe$_5$C$_2$
summary: Quantum phase estimation (QPE) is an underlying technology for extracting the excitation spectra of many-electron systems, yet its practical use on current hardware is hindered by low grid resolution and environmental noises. Here we propose QPE averaged over variable grids (QAVG), a vernier-type approach that combines low-resolution QPE with multiple origin shifts and physically motivated continuous parametrization to reconstruct the spectra accurately. We introduce this approach into an end-to-end workflow for the {\it ab initio}-based model system for a CO molecule adsorbed onto the $χ$-Fe$_5$C$_2$ surface. We perform experiments on Quantinuum H2-2 using both physical QPE circuits and logical QPE circuits encoded in the Steane code with offline bit-flip correction. We demonstrate that QAVG accurately reconstructs the spectra with deviations much smaller than the nominal QPE resolution, even when the noisy histograms are used. The cost landscapes averaged over the shifted grids substantially suppress the local minima arising from the spectral leakage, thereby stabilizing the optimization of trial parameters. These results indicate that QAVG provides a robust route to quantum simulations of correlated spectra toward the era of early-fault-tolerant quantum computers.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a new method called QPE averaged over variable grids (QAVG) for improving quantum phase estimation in many-electron systems, effectively overcoming challenges related to low resolution and noise, and demonstrating its application on a CO molecule using a quantum computer.
AI.motivation: The need for better methods to extract excitation spectra of many-electron systems due to limitations in current quantum phase estimation techniques, specifically low grid resolution and environmental noise.
AI.method: The QAVG method utilizes low-resolution quantum phase estimation combined with origin shifts and continuous parametrization to improve spectrum reconstruction, implemented within an end-to-end workflow for a CO molecule system on a specific surface.
AI.result: QAVG enables accurate reconstruction of excitation spectra with significantly smaller deviations than standard QPE resolution, even in noisy environments. It stabilizes the optimization of parameters by averaging cost landscapes across shifted grids, reducing local minima from spectral leakage.
AI.conclusion: QAVG provides a promising and robust approach for quantum simulations of correlated spectra, paving the way for applications in early-fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Channel-agnostic finite-temperature phase estimation averaged over variable grids: reconstruction of Green's function for dynamical mean-field theory
summary: For treating correlated electronic systems on quantum computers, we propose a quantum-classical hybrid scheme for dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT). In the quantum part of the scheme, we use modified quantum phase estimation (QPE) circuits suitable for the one-particle Green's function (GF) at a finite temperature so that we can extract spectral amplitudes and the excitation energies without knowing the excitation channel invoked at each measurement. In the classical part of the scheme, we adopt an approach that estimates reasonably the GF based on the data collected from the QPE sampling. We dub the approach the QPE averaged over variable grids (QAVG), that may help one to reconstruct the GF via optimization of trial parameters and modeling the probability distributions for various settings of the QPE circuits. We apply the QAVG-DMFT scheme to SrVO$_3$ to demonstrate its validity via numerical simulations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a quantum-classical hybrid method for dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT), utilizing modified quantum phase estimation for efficient extraction of Green's functions at finite temperatures.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to effectively treat correlated electronic systems using quantum computers, aiming to improve the efficiency and accuracy of dynamical mean-field theory.
AI.method: The method involves a quantum part that uses modified quantum phase estimation circuits to obtain spectral amplitudes and excitation energies, combined with a classical approach called QPE averaged over variable grids for estimating the Green's function.
AI.result: The approach, termed QAVG-DMFT, was successfully applied to SrVO$_3$, demonstrating its effectiveness through numerical simulations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed QAVG-DMFT scheme shows promise for efficiently reconstructing Green's functions, thereby advancing the treatment of correlated electronic systems on quantum computers.

title: Tripartite Interactions Induced Strongly Correlated Quantum Emissions
summary: Efficient generation of multiquanta emission is crucial for quantum information processing but remains challenging due to its typical reliance on higher-order quantum processes. Here, we theoretically demonstrate strongly correlated photon-phonon emission enabled by direct tripartite interaction. This interaction facilitates the formation of high-order multiquanta states without more intermediate state transitions, thereby avoiding the suppressed transition rates associated with multiple sequential processes and substantially improving resonant transitions. As a result, high-efficiency strongly correlated even-quanta emission (e.g., two photons and two phonons) can be achieved in the presences of dissipation. Beyond that, we show that introducing two-photon dissipation enables strongly correlated odd-quanta emission (e.g., two photons and one phonon) in the tripartite interaction system by parity-protected suppression of single-photon loss and reconstruction of higher-order multiquanta processes. Our work extends multiquanta emission into the tripartite coupling regime and holds promising potential for applications in hybrid quantum networks.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a theoretical advancement in multiquanta emission by utilizing tripartite interactions to achieve high-efficiency photon-phonon emission, mitigating traditional challenges linked to higher-order quantum processes.
AI.motivation: The need for efficient multiquanta emission in quantum information processing is pivotal yet challenging due to reliance on higher-order quantum processes.
AI.method: The authors demonstrate strongly correlated photon-phonon emission through direct tripartite interactions, facilitating the formation of high-order multiquanta states without sequential transitions.
AI.result: The findings show that high-efficiency even-quanta and odd-quanta emissions can be achieved, even in dissipative environments, by employing two-photon dissipation and parity-protected mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: This research advances multiquanta emission techniques into the tripartite coupling regime, indicating significant potential for future applications in hybrid quantum networks.

title: Finite-key feasibility of geostationary quantum key distribution
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) via geostationary Earth orbit (GEO) satellites offers a compelling route to continuous, continental-scale secure communications. However, operation in this regime entails extreme channel loss and significant background noise, particularly if daylight operation is desired. We present a comprehensive end-to-end feasibility study of a decoy-state BB84 protocol in a GEO downlink configuration, incorporating variable-length finite-key security and tight statistical bounds to expand the achievable positive-key regime. Our analysis encompasses the principal receiver architectures relevant to downlink QKD and employs a physically realistic channel model that captures the dominant loss and noise mechanisms. We evaluate performance across rural, urban, and coastal environments at multiple wavelengths, including visible Fraunhofer absorption minima and the telecom band. Using historical cloud data across Europe, we forecast the annual secret-key yield across the continent. Through a systematic exploration of the high-dimensional parameter space, we identify key trade-offs and performance bottlenecks that determine feasibility. These results establish practical operating thresholds and provide actionable design guidelines for future GEO-QKD missions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a feasibility study for implementing a decoy-state BB84 quantum key distribution protocol using GEO satellites, addressing channel loss, noise, and providing design guidelines for future missions.
AI.motivation: The need for secure communication over large distances using satellite technology despite challenges like extreme channel loss and noise.
AI.method: A comprehensive analysis of a decoy-state BB84 protocol in a GEO downlink scenario, accounting for variable-length finite-key security and diverse receiver architectures.
AI.result: Evaluation of QKD performance in various environments and wavelengths, leading to predictions of key yields across Europe based on historical cloud data.
AI.conclusion: The study identifies critical performance trade-offs and establishes practical thresholds for future GEO-QKD operations.

title: Discrete and Continuous Wigner Functions in Open Quantum Systems: Non-Markovian and Thermodynamic Effects
comment: Ph.D. thesis, Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur (2026)
summary: The central aim of the thesis is to examine how non-classical resources in finite-dimensional quantum systems can be identified, characterized, and protected for practical use in the presence of realistic noise. Using the discrete Wigner functions (DWFs) framework, we introduce negative quantum states and examine how their Wigner negativity, mana, coherence, and teleportation fidelity evolve under unital and non-unital channels, with particular attention to non-Markovian random-telegraph and amplitude-damping dynamics. We also analyze protection strategies based on weak measurement and quantum measurement reversal, showing that these methods can enhance quantum correlations, reduce fidelity deviation, and improve teleportation performance for two-qubit negative states in memory-bearing environments. Moreover, we demonstrate that certain negative states, derived from phase-space point operators, exhibit greater resilience than Bell states in measures of entanglement under non-Markovian noise. Further, this thesis focuses on developing and implementing quantum circuits for generating these states on superconducting hardware and realizing them for the first time on IBM's ibm-Brisbane device. Their preparation is verified using quantum state tomography, demonstrating high fidelity under realistic noise conditions. We propose a teleportation scheme that leverages one of the two-qubit negative quantum states as a resource. Moreover, these two-qubit negative quantum states are also found to perform better than the Bell states for maximal CHSH violation and Fisher information in noisy conditions. We believe that these negative quantum states have the potential to be used in place of the traditional Bell states in scenarios where non-Markovian errors are prevalent. (continued in the PDF)

AI.tldr: This thesis investigates non-classical resources in finite-dimensional quantum systems, focusing on negative quantum states and their resilience to noise.
AI.motivation: To explore non-classical resources for quantum systems that can withstand realistic noise for practical applications.
AI.method: Utilizes discrete Wigner functions to analyze negative states under various noise channels, employs protection strategies, and develops quantum circuits for state generation.
AI.result: Negative states are shown to outperform Bell states in terms of entanglement resilience and teleportation efficiency under non-Markovian noise.
AI.conclusion: Negative quantum states can serve as robust alternatives to traditional Bell states, particularly in environments with significant non-Markovian noise.

title: Treewidth-Aware Gate Cut Selection for Reducing Transpilation Overhead on Superconducting Quantum Devices
summary: On superconducting quantum devices with sparse qubit connectivity, transpilation of long-range two-qubit interactions inserts additional SWAP gates, increasing hardware cost and execution error. Gate cutting via quasi-probability decomposition (QPD) can remove a selected two-qubit gate and thereby reduce routing overhead, but its sampling cost makes cut placement critical. We propose TW2S, a graph-only two-stage gate-cut selection method that operates on the circuit interaction graph without backend-specific transpilation at selection time. Stage 1 analyzes a min-fill elimination trace and scores edges by their contribution to a treewidth upper bound. Stage 2 ranks the resulting candidates by edge betweenness centrality with a degree penalty to identify routing bottlenecks. Across grid, Watts-Strogatz, barbell, and stochastic block model benchmarks transpiled to IBM's FakeSherbrooke backend, TW2S consistently outperforms random cut selection when the interaction graph contains identifiable sparse cuts. The advantage is governed not by absolute graph density but by moderate community structure and accessible inter-community edges. We further derive a mean-squared-error breakeven condition showing that, under a shared total shot budget, QPD is beneficial only when the ECR reduction is large enough and the signal strength is sufficient. Under an expanded per-subcircuit budget the signal-strength requirement is substantially relaxed. In noisy simulations of the J1-J2 transverse-field Ising model, TW2S achieves $Δ$ECR = 47 for n = 8, compared with approximately 9 for random selection, and yields lower estimation error than the uncut baseline in the tested strong-signal regime, with larger gains at increased shot budgets. These results position graph-structural cut selection as a practical compiler-side tool for turning circuit cutting into a targeted routing-reduction strategy.

AI.tldr: TW2S is a method for optimizing two-qubit gate cuts in quantum circuits that improves efficiency without backend-specific transpilation, outperforming random selections in various graph models.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the inefficiencies introduced by additional SWAP gates in superconducting quantum devices with sparse qubit connectivity.
AI.method: TW2S operates in two stages: the first analyzes the circuit interaction graph to score edges based on their contribution to the treewidth upper bound; the second ranks potential cuts by their edge betweenness centrality, factoring in a degree penalty.
AI.result: TW2S consistently outperforms random cut selection across diverse benchmarks, showing significant improvements in estimation error and effective routing under increased shot budgets.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that graph-structural cut selection can effectively reduce routing overhead in quantum circuits, making it a valuable tool for compiler-side optimizations.

title: Bound-state-protected phase metrology for a quantum emitter in a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger bath
summary: We study local phase estimation for a single quantum emitter coupled to a bosonic Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) bath within a microscopic lattice model. Dimerization opens a central gap supporting an in-gap emitter-bath bound state, which suppresses complete relaxation of the emitter coherence. A Dyson-equation analysis yields the local bath Green's function, the in-gap bound-state condition, and the emitter residue controlling the retained phase information. The phase quantum Fisher information links gap formation, detuning, and emitter-bath coupling to the post-transient metrological response. At resonance, stronger coupling enhances transient hybridization but reduces the retained signal by lowering the emitter weight in the bound state. Away from resonance, late-time averages, retention times, and useful interrogation windows track how phase-information protection weakens as the emitter is tuned toward and beyond the band edge. A uniform-chain control shows that the retained signal disappears when the gap closes. In the bulk local-coupling geometry considered here, the response is insensitive to the sign of the dimerization, so the protocol probes spectral-gap physics and bound-state support rather than the SSH winding sector.

AI.tldr: The paper explores local phase estimation in a quantum emitter coupled to a dimerized bosonic SSH bath, revealing impacts on coherence and phase information retention based on system parameters and spectral characteristics.
AI.motivation: To understand the mechanisms by which a single quantum emitter retains phase information when interacting with a bosonic SSH bath, particularly through the effects of dimerization and bound states.
AI.method: The authors employ a microscopic lattice model, using Dyson-equation analysis to derive the local bath Green's function, in-gap bound-state conditions, and emitter residue relevant to phase information.
AI.result: The analysis shows that at resonance, stronger emitter-bath coupling enhances hybridization but decreases retained phase signal, while away from resonance, retention times and averages indicate how phase information protection diminishes as the emitter approaches the band edge.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest that spectral-gap characteristics dominate the coherence retention dynamics, and the response does not depend on the dimerization sign, indicating a broader exploration of spectral-gap physics over the SSH winding sector.

title: Non-Perturbative Closed Form for the Typical Bipartite Mutual Information of Haar-Random States
comment: 5 pages. This is a companion paper to our simultaneous submission with a title "Exact Geometric Typicality and Bipartite Entanglement from the Projected Central Limit Theorem on Hyperspheres"
summary: The average bipartite quantum mutual information $\langle I(A{:}B)\rangle$ of Haar-random pure states can be expressed exactly through Page's formula in terms of digamma functions. We show that this quantity admits a single non-perturbative closed form: $\langle I(A{:}B)\rangle = (d_A^2-1)(d_B^2-1)\,\mathcal{G}(d_A,d_B,d_E)$, where $\mathcal{G}$ is given by an explicit convergent integral over a Bose--Einstein kernel. The overall factor $(d_A^2-1)(d_B^2-1)=\dim[\mathfrak{su}(d_A)]\cdot\dim[\mathfrak{su}(d_B)]$ is exact, not merely asymptotic. The asymptotic expansion of $\mathcal{G}$ in $1/N$ yields a Bernoulli-factorised series whose coefficients involve $ζ(1{-}2k)$; this series diverges, and our integral is its exact Borel sum. The integral representation also makes $\langle I\rangle < (d_A^2{-}1)(d_B^2{-}1)/(2N)$ manifest via a scale-inversion symmetry of the kernel. Our derivation traces the mutual information's structure to an exact decomposition of Page's entropy into a diagonal (Dirichlet) contribution and a Schur-majorisation eigenvalue correction, whose assembly into the mutual information cleanly separates classical from quantum correlations.

AI.tldr: The paper provides an exact expression for the average bipartite quantum mutual information of Haar-random pure states using Page's formula. It presents a closed form involving digamma functions and a convergent integral over a Bose–Einstein kernel, demonstrating a clear separation of classical and quantum correlations.
AI.motivation: To derive an exact formulation of average bipartite quantum mutual information in Haar-random pure states and understand its structure through Page's entropy.
AI.method: The authors express the average mutual information using an integral representation involving a Bose–Einstein kernel and derive a non-perturbative closed form. They analyze asymptotic behaviors and demonstrate scale-inversion symmetry.
AI.result: The closed form of mutual information is given by $ ig(d_A^2-1)(d_B^2-1) ig\,	ext{G}(d_A,d_B,d_E)$, with the integral providing an exact Borel sum of an asymptotic series that diverges, along with a clear upper bound.
AI.conclusion: The mutual information formulation cleanly divides classical and quantum contributions by connecting it to a structured decomposition of Page's entropy.

title: Exact Geometric Typicality and Bipartite Entanglement from the Projected Central Limit Theorem on Hyperspheres
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure. This is a companion paper to our simultaneous submission with a title "Non-Perturbative Closed Form for the Typical Bipartite Mutual Information of Haar-Random States"
summary: Starting from the exact Projected Central Limit Theorem on hyperspheres, we rederive the Beta distribution for subsystem occupation probabilities and Lubkin's purity formula from elementary hyperspherical moments, quantifying the finite-size ``platykurtic'' suppression of tails relative to the Gaussian approximation used in standard eigenstate-thermalization and typicality treatments. Our main new result concerns the bipartite quantum mutual information $\langle I(A{:}B)\rangle$ for Haar-random pure states. We show that its full asymptotic expansion in $1/N$ admits a Bernoulli-factorized form in which every order $k \ge 1$ carries the symmetric factor $(d_A^{2k}-1)(d_B^{2k}-1)$ and all higher odd-order corrections vanish identically. Through an exact algebraic reorganization of Page's formula (conjectured in Ref.~\cite{Page1993} and subsequently proven~\cite{Foong1994, SanchezRuiz1995, Sen1996}), we establish that the leading finite-size correction separates into a dominant $\mathfrak{su}(d_A) \otimes \mathfrak{su}(d_B)$ bipartite quantum coherence contribution $(d_A^2 - 1)(d_B^2 - 1)/(2N)$ and a subtracted classical-probability (Cartan $\otimes$ Cartan) contribution $(d_A - 1)(d_B - 1)/(2N)$, and we trace this separation to the difference between diagonal and eigenvalue entropies via Schur's majorisation theorem, with the dimensional counts $(d-1)$ and $(d^2-1)$ acquiring meaning through the Cartan structure of the generalised Bloch decomposition. These results admit a single non-perturbative closed form: the exact typical mutual information factors as $\langle I(A{:}B)\rangle = (d_A^2-1)(d_B^2-1)\,\mathcal{G}(d_A,d_B,d_E)$, with $\mathcal{G}$ given by an explicit Bose--Einstein integral whose asymptotic expansion in $1/N$ reproduces the Bernoulli series.

AI.tldr: The study provides a detailed examination of the bipartite quantum mutual information for Haar-random pure states by utilizing the Projected Central Limit Theorem and deriving important results related to finite-size corrections.
AI.motivation: To understand the behavior of subsystem occupation probabilities and mutual information in quantum systems, particularly in the context of finite-size effects.
AI.method: Employing the Projected Central Limit Theorem on hyperspheres to derive the Beta distribution, along with an algebraic reorganization of Page's formula, to analyze the asymptotic expansion of mutual information in terms of system dimensions.
AI.result: The leading finite-size correction can be decomposed into contributions from quantum coherence and classical probability, revealing that higher odd-order corrections vanish and leading to a Bernoulli-factorized form of mutual information.
AI.conclusion: The typical mutual information can be succinctly expressed as a product involving an explicit Bose–Einstein integral, with its asymptotic behavior reflecting the derived structural forms.

title: Quantum algorithms for density functional theory with minimal readout
summary: While quantum computers have shown significant promise for electronic structure calculations, their potential to accelerate density functional theory (DFT) calculations remains unclear. In this work, we present a qubit-efficient encoding scheme for wavefunctions in Kohn--Sham (KS) DFT, together with a quantum algorithm that computes all occupied orbitals simultaneously. We further show that our algorithm is particularly well suited to the Harris functional, enabling the total energy to be evaluated with a potential exponential speedup over classical approaches by entirely avoiding the costly readout of the electronic density. In addition, we propose a second method for achieving self-consistent DFT calculations using multiple copies of the wavefunction, which likewise circumvents density readout. The applicability of our algorithms is demonstrated through several numerical examples, and their efficiency is compared with that of existing approaches.

AI.tldr: Developed a qubit-efficient quantum algorithm for Kohn-Sham DFT that computes occupied orbitals and total energy with potential exponential speedup, avoiding electronic density readout.
AI.motivation: To explore the potential of quantum computing to enhance the efficiency of DFT calculations, which are computationally demanding in classical settings.
AI.method: Introduced an encoding scheme for wavefunctions in KS DFT and a quantum algorithm that simultaneously computes all occupied orbitals, particularly effective with the Harris functional; proposed a secondary method using multiple wavefunction copies for self-consistency.
AI.result: Demonstrated improved efficiency and potential exponential speedup in DFT calculations, with successful application in numerical examples.
AI.conclusion: Our algorithms present a promising direction for leveraging quantum computing in density functional theory, improving scalability over classical methods.

title: Incompleteness is necessary for activation of nonlocality without entanglement
summary: A set of orthogonal product states is said to exhibit "quantum nonlocality without entanglement" if it is locally indistinguishable, i.e. no sequence of local operations and classical communication (LOCC) can perfectly discriminate the states. Building on this foundational idea, recent studies have highlighted the phenomenon of "genuine activation of hidden nonlocality", where a set of initially distinguishable orthogonal states becomes locally indistinguishable through orthogonality-preserving LOCC transformations. In this letter, we establish that any complete orthogonal product basis that is initially locally distinguishable remains so under all orthogonality-preserving local projective measurements, thereby ruling out activation via orthogonality-preserving local projective measurements and classical communication. We further introduce and formalise the notions of "strongly local sets", namely locally distinguishable sets that remain non-activable under all bipartitions. Interestingly, the study of "local activability" of distinguishable sets is useful to characterise the boundary between LOCC distinguishability and its irreversible loss in multipartite systems. Our results provide a rigorous structural understanding of local-to-nonlocal transitions in quantum state discrimination.

AI.tldr: The paper explores quantum nonlocality without entanglement, establishing that orthogonal product bases can maintain local distinguishability under certain measurements and introducing 'strongly local sets'.
AI.motivation: The goal is to understand the transition between locally distinguishable and indistinguishable states in quantum systems, particularly in relation to nonlocality without entanglement.
AI.method: The authors analyze complete orthogonal product bases and their behavior under orthogonality-preserving local projective measurements, defining the concept of 'strongly local sets'.
AI.result: The research shows that initially locally distinguishable bases cannot become indistinguishable through the defined local operations, and it articulates the concept of strong local sets.
AI.conclusion: The findings enhance our understanding of local-to-nonlocal transitions and provide critical insight into the structure of state discrimination in multipartite quantum systems.

title: Resolving the phase space
summary: Quantum tomography can reconstruct fine phase-space structures that are not necessarily resolved by measurement itself. We show that the effective resolution of tomography is determined by a sampling operator linked to the Gram matrix of the measurement, which defines the experimentally accessible degrees of freedom and reconstruction bandwidth of the quantum state. Acting analogously to a transfer function in imaging, this operator provides an operational criterion for distinguishing genuinely resolved quantum features from artefacts induced by incomplete sampling or reconstruction assumptions. Reconstruction in the Gram eigenbasis emerges as an efficient measurement-adapted compression of the tomographic problem. Within finite frame theory, the same structure appears naturally as the frame operator. Our results establish a resolution-based framework for quantum tomography relevant for contemporary experiments probing highly structured nonclassical states.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a framework for quantum tomography that enhances resolution by analyzing sampling operators linked to the Gram matrix, allowing for the effective reconstruction of quantum states.
AI.motivation: To improve the resolution in quantum tomography and distinguish genuine features from artefacts due to measurement limitations.
AI.method: The study utilizes a sampling operator based on the Gram matrix of measurements, analogous to an imaging transfer function, and reconstructs states in the Gram eigenbasis for efficient measurement adaptation.
AI.result: Establishes a resolution-based framework that allows for the effective identification of genuinely resolved quantum features while accounting for artefacts from incomplete sampling.
AI.conclusion: The findings are significant for contemporary quantum experiments investigating structured nonclassical states.

title: Chain rules for conditional entropies in quantum cryptography: limitations and improvements
summary: Security proofs in quantum cryptography rely on conditional entropies. In a many-round protocol, their estimation is a challenging task; one must account for the most general attacks by an eavesdropper, including those that are not independently and identically distributed (i.i.d.) across all rounds. Chain rules address this problem by relating the conditional entropy of a structured, but non-i.i.d. process to a sum of entropy contributions from each round. They are a key ingredient in entropy accumulation theorems (EATs), which provide a versatile security proof framework for many protocols in quantum cryptography. Recently, chain rules in the setting of trusted devices have lead to tight i.i.d. reductions at a finite number of rounds, and whether analogous results can be recovered in the device-independent (DI) setting has not been addressed. Surprisingly, we show that a natural tightening of the chain rule of Dupuis et al. [Commun. Math. Phys. 379, 867-913, (2020)] that would answer this question affirmatively cannot hold, highlighting a limitation of the current DI security proof approach. Nonetheless, we show that an intermediate improvement is possible by proving a new chain rule in this setting. Following the framework of Arqand et al. [Phys. Rev. X 15, 041013 (2025)], we use our chain rule to provide a slightly tighter version of the Rényi EAT in certain contexts. In addition, we provide a self-contained framework that unifies existing chain rules and compares their applications, framing our results in a broader context.

AI.tldr: This paper examines chain rules applied to conditional entropies in quantum cryptography, particularly focusing on the limitations in device-independent settings and providing new insights for entropy accumulation theorems.
AI.motivation: The need to enhance security proofs in quantum cryptography, particularly in non-i.i.d. scenarios, motivates the exploration of chain rules that can effectively analyze conditional entropies across many rounds of interaction.
AI.method: The authors propose a new chain rule in a device-independent setting that serves as an intermediate improvement over existing methods, while also providing a unified framework for comparing different chain rules.
AI.result: The new chain rule allows for a slightly tighter version of the Rényi entropy accumulation theorem in specific contexts, addressing limitations identified in previous approaches.
AI.conclusion: The study highlights both the challenges and potential improvements in the analysis of quantum cryptographic protocols, emphasizing the importance of the introduced chain rule in the broader context of security proofs.

title: Adaptive Stabilizer State Fidelity Certification
comment: 24 pages, 5 figures and 2 tables. Comments are welcome
summary: Certifying the fidelity of a prepared state to a target stabilizer state is a fundamental task in quantum information processing. Ref. [Phys. Rev. A 99, 042337 (2019)] gave the optimal worst-case lower bound from one fixed stabilizer generator gauge, but gauge dependence can leave a large fidelity ambiguity. We develop an adaptive extension that reports the full certified fidelity interval. First, for a single gauge, we derive the complementary optimal worst-case upper bound. We then formulate gauge selection as an adaptive design problem in which each round solves exact endpoint linear programs and chooses a new gauge by a witness elimination policy. We prove monotonic tightening, exact recovery once all nontrivial stabilizers are covered, and the worst-case necessity of full coverage. Finally, we identify structured syndrome distributions for which adaptivity beats this exponential benchmark, and we numerically confirm faster concentration.

AI.tldr: This paper enhances the certification of fidelity to stabilizer states by developing an adaptive method that provides a complete interval of certified fidelity, overcoming gauge dependence and ambiguity.
AI.motivation: The fundamental task of certifying the fidelity of quantum states is hindered by gauge dependence, leading to potential ambiguities in fidelity estimation.
AI.method: An adaptive design approach for gauge selection is proposed, solving endpoint linear programs in each round and employing a witness elimination strategy to select new gauges, thus deriving both upper and lower bounds.
AI.result: The method yields a complete interval of certified fidelity and proves that adaptivity can outperform traditional exponential benchmarks in specific syndrome distributions.
AI.conclusion: The developed adaptive scheme achieves a tighter fidelity estimation and guarantees recovery when all nontrivial stabilizers are accounted for, demonstrating significant improvements in efficiency.

title: Indistinguishability of photonic qubits emitted from trapped $^{40}$Ca$^+$ ions via pulsed excitation
summary: We investigate the indistinguishability of Raman photons generated from two trapped $^{40}$Ca$^+$ ions using few-nanosecond excitation pulses. We elucidate how spontaneous scattering back to the initial state affects Hong-Ou-Mandel interference. We identify the mean number of back-decays as a measurable single-emitter quantity that correlates with achievable interference visibility of photons from two identical emitters.

AI.tldr: This study explores the indistinguishability of Raman photons from trapped $^{40}$Ca$^+$ ions and its effect on Hong-Ou-Mandel interference.
AI.motivation: Understanding the indistinguishability of photons is crucial for quantum communication and computing applications, particularly in enhancing interference effects.
AI.method: The authors investigated the effect of spontaneous scattering on Hong-Ou-Mandel interference using few-nanosecond excitation pulses on two trapped ions.
AI.result: They demonstrated that the mean number of back-decays is a significant parameter, influencing the interference visibility of the photons emitted from the two identical emitters.
AI.conclusion: This study provides insights into how single-emitter characteristics can impact the indistinguishability of quantum optical sources, important for future quantum technologies.

title: Gate Parameter Lee-Yang Zeros and Dynamical Phases in Quantum Circuits
summary: We propose gate-parameter Lee-Yang zeros of Loschmidt amplitudes as probes of dynamical phases in finite quantum circuits. We illustrate this approach using a brickwork model, where the time evolution is generated by repeated application of a Floquet operator. The Loschmidt amplitude can be expressed as a rational function of the gate parameters. At fixed system size and large circuit depth, its zeros in one complexified gate parameter, with the other parameter held fixed, condense onto limiting curves. We show that these curves comprise a universal component governed by equimodular Floquet eigenvalues, as described by the Beraha-Kahane-Weiss theorem, together with state-dependent contributions controlled by the overlap of eigenstate of the Floquet operator with the initial state. As one of the parameters is varied, the set of zeros reorganizes abruptly, providing a finite-qubit diagnostic of a dynamical phase transition. This mechanism does not rely on integrability: while integrability enables an exact calculation of the Loschmidt amplitude, the condensation of zeros follows from spectral competition and local unitarity alone.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces gate-parameter Lee-Yang zeros of Loschmidt amplitudes as a method to probe dynamical phases in finite quantum circuits, revealing transitions through the behavior of zeros in circuit parameters.
AI.motivation: To investigate dynamical phases in quantum circuits and develop a diagnostic tool that does not depend on integrability.
AI.method: Utilization of gate-parameter Lee-Yang zeros of Loschmidt amplitudes with a brickwork model governed by a Floquet operator, examining zeros' organization in the parameter space.
AI.result: The zeros condense onto universal curves dictated by Floquet eigenvalues, showcasing abrupt reorganizations that signal dynamical phase transitions as parameters change.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides insights into dynamical transitions in finite qubit systems without relying solely on integrability, emphasizing the role of spectral competition and local unitarity.

title: Toward Practical Two-Way Covert Communication
summary: We study two-way covert communication schemes, where information is transmitted by passively modulating a reflected signal back to the source. We consider optical systems, described by quantum bosonic channels. While broadband classical and quantum light sources offer high covert throughput in theory, the associated mode-matching and phase-synchronization requirements make them impractical. Therefore, we employ a narrowband laser source to experimentally demonstrate a proof-of-concept two-way covert communication system, where the adversary is assumed to be quantum-capable. Furthermore, we propose a correlator-based receiver that attains the broadband gain offered by a quantum light source without the need for precise mode matching.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates two-way covert communication using quantum bosonic channels and proposes a practical system using narrowband lasers, alongside a correlator-based receiver for enhanced performance.
AI.motivation: The exploration of covert communication schemes that can transmit information stealthily is crucial, particularly when the adversary has quantum capabilities.
AI.method: The study utilized narrowband laser sources to create an experimental two-way covert communication system, eliminating the impracticalities of broadband sources in terms of mode matching and synchronization.
AI.result: The experimental results validate the proof-of-concept for the covert communication system, demonstrating effective communication even in the presence of quantum-capable adversaries.
AI.conclusion: A correlator-based receiver can achieve the benefits of broadband gain without stringent requirements, making the system more feasible in practical applications.

title: Claim against Measurement: Statistical Artefacts in Quantum Error Mitigation Benchmarks
summary: QEM is widely regarded as a plausible bridge from NISQ devices to FTQC. Yet the empirical studies used to assess the effectiveness of QEM techniques on concrete problems have received comparatively little scrutiny with respect to the validity of their conclusions. We systematically review 81 recent QEM papers using an eight-criterion framework covering statistical rigour, reproducibility, and reporting quality. Among the applicable papers, only 15 (25%) use inferential methods, while 25 (42%) report uncertainty only descriptively, without testing whether the claimed effects are statistically supported. To demonstrate the consequences of these omissions, we use ZNE as a representative and widely used case study and identify two compounding sources of artefacts in current QEM benchmarks. First, we observe parameter sensitivity: in a 132-configuration sweep, implicitly assumed choices such as scale factors, extrapolation method, and hardware calibration are not merely incidental but active, with variations changing conclusions from statistically significant improvement to statistically significant degradation. Second, we identify a drift-induced effectiveness illusion: in a 72-hour longitudinal study on real hardware, temporal drift alone can make the same ZNE configuration exhibit an effect size more than three times as large, depending solely on when it is executed, and also drastically reduces the effective number of independent observations. These findings do not imply that QEM methods are intrinsically unsound; rather, they show that current evaluation practice can make mitigation performance appear more robust than the evidence warrants. We therefore propose minimum reporting standards for QEM evaluations, including explicit parameter documentation, robustness checks, longitudinal drift assessment, and inferential statistical testing with effect-size reporting.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews 81 recent QEM studies, revealing significant issues in statistical rigor and reporting. Only 25% use inferential methods. It highlights parameter sensitivity and drift-induced biases in current benchmarks, proposing improved reporting standards.
AI.motivation: To assess the empirical validity of QEM techniques in bridging NISQ devices to FTQC, as previous studies showed a lack of scrutiny on their conclusions.
AI.method: A systematic review of 81 QEM papers using an eight-criterion framework focusing on statistical rigor, reproducibility, and reporting quality.
AI.result: Only 15 papers (25%) used inferential methods; 25 (42%) provided only descriptive uncertainty reports. Identified issues include parameter sensitivity affecting outcomes and drift-induced biases in effectiveness measures.
AI.conclusion: Current evaluation practices may exaggerate QEM techniques' performance robustness. The paper proposes minimum reporting standards to enhance clarity and reliability in QEM evaluations.

title: Verifying Adversarial Robustness in Quantum Machine Learning: from theory to physical validation via a software tool
